S021.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
S021.description: Symptoms where speech or thought appears scattered and difficult to follow due to a lack of logical or consistent flow.

subtypes.Derailment or Loose Associations: A speech pattern of switching rapidly from one topic to another with no logical connection between thoughts.
subtypes.Tangentiality: Speech that deviates entirely from the question and fails to answer directly.
subtypes.Incoherence or Word Salad: Severe fragmentation of speech and sentence structure, making it nearly impossible to understand.
subtypes.Neologisms: Using made-up words that have meaning only to the individual.
subtypes.Clang Associations: Speech governed by sounds, such as rhyming, rather than the meaning of words.

S022.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
S022.description: A state where behavior and motor control are severely disturbed, appearing as movements or reactions inappropriate to the situation.

subtypes.Childlike Silliness: Inappropriate, childish, or illogical behavior appearing in situations.
subtypes.Stupor: No psychomotor activity; not actively relating to environment.
subtypes.Catalepsy: Passive induction of a posture held against gravity.
subtypes.Waxy Flexibility: Slight, even resistance to positioning by examiner.
subtypes.Mutism: No, or very little, verbal response despite the ability to speak.
subtypes.Negativism: Opposition or no response to instructions or external stimuli without apparent motive.
subtypes.Posturing: Spontaneous and active maintenance of a posture against gravity.
subtypes.Mannerism: Odd, circumstantial caricature of normal actions.
subtypes.Agitation: Excessive motor activity without obvious external cause.
subtypes.Grimacing: Contorted facial expressions irrelevant to the situation.

symptom.disease_info: Schizophrenia is a chronic psychotic disorder characterized by disturbances in thought, perception, emotion, and behavior, with core features including delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking or behavior, and negative symptoms such as reduced motivation and social withdrawal. Onset typically occurs in late adolescence to early adulthood and is usually preceded by a prodromal phase of functional decline, odd beliefs, or subtle cognitive and social changes. The course is often relapsing and remitting or chronically persistent, with significant impairment in occupational, academic, and social functioning if untreated. It is distinguished from mood disorders with psychotic features by the presence of psychosis outside of mood episodes, and from brief or substance-induced psychotic disorders by its longer duration and characteristic decline in functioning.

patient.personality: Marcus is a steady, pragmatic man who takes pride in his disciplined work habits, love of sports, and low-key enjoyment of cooking and community involvement.
patient.stressor: Roughly a year before his evaluation, Marcus was involved in a minor work-related traffic incident that, while causing no serious physical injury, shook his longstanding confidence in his driving and led to a brief medical leave and intensive safety review at his company. For a man who had built his identity on being a reliable, rule-following driver, the scrutiny, fear of losing his commercial license, and the realization of his own aging body stirred up significant anxiety and shame that he mostly kept to himself. Over the following months, coworkers and friends at the community center noticed that he began acting in ways that were markedly out of character—showing up to the depot at odd hours, abruptly abandoning routes, pacing or making sudden, purposeless movements in the yard, and behaving in confusing ways during routine tasks that jeopardized safety and ultimately led to suspension from driving duties. As his functioning deteriorated further at home and in social settings, with his erratic actions alarming neighbors and his inability to manage daily routines threatening his independence, his sister and union representative accompanied him to a psychiatric clinic, worried that something far more serious than stress over the accident was driving these drastic behavioral changes.
patient.chief_complaint: “People keep telling me I’m acting strange and doing things that don’t fit what’s going on, but I don’t understand why I’m doing it.”

S021.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
S021.description: Symptoms where speech or thought appears scattered and difficult to follow due to a lack of logical or consistent flow.
S021.manifestation: When I try to explain to my sister what happened on the route, I start out talking about the truck, then I jump to the Cowboys game, then the food pantry, and by the time I’m done I can see on her face that none of it connects and I never actually answered her question, even though in my head it all fits together somehow.

S022.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
S022.description: A state where behavior and motor control are severely disturbed, appearing as movements or reactions inappropriate to the situation.
S022.manifestation: I’ll be at the depot or in my apartment and suddenly find myself pacing back and forth, waving my arms or freezing in a weird stance like I’m checking mirrors on an invisible truck, and even when people tell me to sit down or stop, it’s like my body just keeps doing its own thing and I can’t match how I’m acting to what’s really going on around me.
